name: FN-DSA (Rust, Falcon-based post-quantum signatures)
workload: Single FN-DSA/512 (Falcon) key generation, signature generation and verification, measured in CPU clock cycles, compared in prose against OpenSSL's RSA-2048 signing/verification cost on the same CPU families
claimed_speedup: ~8x faster signature generation than OpenSSL RSA-2048 on ARM Cortex-A76; roughly RSA-2048-verify parity on x86_64; keygen and signing described as 'many times faster' / '2.5x faster' than RSA-2048 depending on operation
compiler_and_flags: Rust 1.97.1 (rustc), AVX2 auto-detected at runtime on x86_64, NEON on aarch64; OpenSSL build/version/flags used for the comparison are not stated
hardware: Intel i5-8259U (Coffee Lake); ARM Cortex-A76 (Broadcom BCM2712C1); SiFive U74 (RISC-V)
tradeoffs: Pure Rust with runtime AVX2/NEON dispatch; a feature-parity C port exists (pornin/c-fn-dsa) with similar performance; Falcon/FN-DSA keys and signatures are larger than RSA/ECDSA equivalents and keygen is comparatively expensive (though far faster than RSA-2048 keygen); floating-point signing requires care for constant-time behavior
caveats: The OpenSSL comparison is a prose claim ('about 8 times faster') without a side-by-side OpenSSL cycle table on the same benchmark page, and no OpenSSL build flags are given, so this is a first-party claim with partial methodology, not a fully reproducible A/B benchmark; FN-DSA itself is still a pre-standardization draft implementation (final NIST FIPS 206 not yet published), so behavior may change
found_via: gh search code "faster than OpenSSL" "Ed25519" (hit README prose); corroborated via crates.io q=falcon listing (fn-dsa, fn-dsa-sign, fn-dsa-vrfy, fn-dsa-kgen crates)

name: ocaml-curve448 (C backend: X448/Ed448)
workload: Single-operation X448 Diffie-Hellman key exchange and Ed448/Ed448ph sign+verify of a 64-byte message; best-of-three 1-second runs measured against `openssl speed` on the same machine
claimed_speedup: X448 key exchange ~1.0-1.24x faster (130us vs 133us on Apple M1 Pro; 93us vs 115us on AMD Ryzen AI 9 HX PRO 370); Ed448 sign up to ~2.3x faster on the Ryzen box (48us vs 111us) but ~7% slower on the M1 (64us vs 60us); Ed448 verify 1.3-1.5x slower than OpenSSL because the C backend is constant-time while OpenSSL uses variable-time double-scalar multiplication (derived from page data)
compiler_and_flags: C backend built via dune's release profile with GCC or Clang (exact flags not stated); OCaml 5.4.1 / 5.5.1; compared against OpenSSL 3.6.4 via `openssl speed`
hardware: Apple M1 Pro (macOS); AMD Ryzen AI 9 HX PRO 370 (Linux)
stars_or_usage: 0 stars (new project, first published this week)
tradeoffs: C backend field arithmetic is derived from fiat-crypto (formally verified) with code from BoringSSL and tiny_sha3; the pure-OCaml default backend is much slower than both the C backend and OpenSSL (e.g. 374us vs 130us/133us for X448 on the M1); package is not yet published to opam
caveats: Results are mixed, not a clean win: OpenSSL is faster for Ed448 sign on Apple M1 and always faster for Ed448 verify (by design, due to constant-time execution); the project is brand new with 0 stars and no independent review; exact compiler version/flags for the C backend are not stated, so this falls short of tier A/B despite stated CPU models and OpenSSL version
